politician as Mr. Cross should have committed so gross a blunder. It is really not unconceiv- able at all; it is not even surprising. There is no more familiar phenomenon than the sudden collapse of artificial reputations; and, both in the world of politics and of business, the man who acquires a sort of suserstitious fame for sagacity is sure, sooner or later, irretrievably to compromise himself The safe man of the Cabinet has brought forward a bill which does every one of those things that he solemnly assured Parliament last August it should not do, and which fails to accomplish any one of those purposes for which it was introduced. It has already opened the door to jobbery and speculation of the most shameless character. It would, if it became law, benefit no person who was not a shareholder in Abe water com- panies. It would impose new burdens on the ratepayers; It would not guarantee a supply of pure water for the metropolis; it would create fresh patronage for the Government, and .new opportunities of nepotism and cor- ruption. Mr. Cross is one of thoss persons whose show of defiant firmness immediately vanishes if be is fairly "collared." He swims with the stream and shouts with the mob. He will do anything with a crowd behind him; but directly the crowd falls away, he falls too. He is a precise type of that Minister whom our new democratic system may be expected to develop in profusion, and is completely at the mercy of the public opinion of the hour. The vilest criminal who was ever sentenced to death has but to induce the democracy to shout loudly enough against his sentence, and commuted that sen- tence will certainly be. Mr. Cross is just the kind of statesman who invites manipulation. In the matter of the present measure he has been " got at" by the companies; it now re- main for him to be "got at " by the ratepay- ers and the public generally. BIRTH.—At the Sale Police Ceurt, on Sarah Mai y Pavitt. domestic servant, was brought up on the charge of concealing the birth of her child at sale on tLe Intl, of March last. It appeared bole the .e.T.ldence that the defeorlant woe in '

the employ of Mrs Ferns, a widow living In Wardle-road Sale. Mrs. Ferns had noticed Om condition of the defendant.. , and accused her of it, but she denied it. On Tharsday she ' went about her work in the usual way, and on Friday witness , noticA it change in her appearance. On going up into her , bedroom and looking under wane clothes she found the dead body of a turtle child. There had been no preparations made. She AI once sent tor a nurse, Mrs. Elizabeth Milne, and, Inspector Leighton. and P. C. Senior. She denied the charge, and was remanded ur.til Monday. on hail. He had no hesita- tion in saying that he had killed two animels since he came Into the neighl.urbood. div.head: TIIE EXAMIN ER.
div.p: TIIE EXAMIN ER.
SATURDAY, MARCH 27, IMO.
THE HOME SECRETARY AND THE DEFENCE OF THE GOVERNMENT.

The tact has not escaped the attention of else- tioneerent that the Home Secretary, the "practical man of the Cabinet," whose &mines, it ehoul I be to attend to horse rather than to foreign affairs, hee, atom he entered upon the struggle for re-election in South-West Lancashire, proved, by the absence from his platform addresses of all reference to home mat- ter. that the Government bee nothing in the way of borne legielation to be proud of. Mr. Cross hae at his elbow Colonel John Ireland Blackbarne, who cries " Ditto" to all the utterancee of the Home Secretary. This happy pasr are now moving about the division, ! devoting themnelven to proving that the Government in the Eastern dispute h. benoi theproverbial innocent white ben. Mr. Cross started hie defence of the foreign policy of the Government at Warrington, end he has repeated him, elf at St. Helens, Southport. and other places. The local Tories have exercised themselves in showering praises upon him without stint, and have eoniforted thenowlvee with the assurance that the hon. gentlemen's defence of the Government's foreign policy ia unanswerable, deepite the clinching arguluente of Lord Hartington and others to the contrary. Mr. Crone at Warring- ton attributed the disturbances in the East to the bad government of Turkey and the fomenting of innurrec- ! tine by Bonilla. The policy of the Government, he said, was not the maintenauce of Turkey in her bad rule whilst they opposed Remits seeking to errors possession of provinces in which alms was fomenting insurrection. He aaid, also, there was a compact . between the three Emperors of Europe for coercing ! Turkey to mend her had Government, and that England reftitted to join that compact because coercion meant war. The British Government, he observed, I : intimated that they would not countenance the suit-1 ! rule in Turkey, and they told the three Emperorsl they would give a solemn warning to Turkey to improve the Government of her pruritic., but that they could not coerce her, and that : nothing could induce England to fight for ! her even if it came to the destruction of her, empire. On that ground Mr. Cross claimed that the ! policy of the Government had been one of pese,e and : not of war, though in the next breath he remarked, that the Government gave Russia ti understand that' if she invaded Turkey the inv./don would be looked I upon as treaty-breaking, a thing that could not be done without the consent of France and Austria, and that England would be compelled to go to war on that account, if called upon by theve two powers to do Now, which of these two statements are we to accept —the one that England would not go to war even if Turkey was destroyed, or the statement that if Russia invaded Turkey England would he compelled to go to war if called upon by Austria anti France? Which statement, as both are from the lips of the Home &cemetery, will satisfy the electors Mr. Cross went on to say that when war did break out the English Government gave Bemis to under- stand that there were British interest* at stake, namely, the Sue. Canal, Egypt, the occupation of Con- stantinople, and the peewee of the Dardenellea, interference with which by Rumba would be resented by England. When Rumba and Turkey endeavouredl to come to an agreement at St. Stefano, Mr. Cruse said the English Government protested. The Rae. tans, he remarked, were at that time advancing, and their goal was Consmntinople, from which they could not have been driven out if they had onee got 112. He maintained, too, that peace had been pre- nerved in Europe, though there was actual war, by the firm attitude shown by the Government, and Gist the Crimean War would never have happened if there bad been no hesitation. Rusks is simply made the bogie, and the Home Secretary would seem to think that the people of Warrington, St. Helens, and other parts of South-West Lancashire are capable of being hoodwinked with any kind of twaddle. They are, we fancy, too much alive to the fact that there is " a lying spirit &broad." If Mr. Grose is unable to tell the story of the Government's eareer without con- tradicting himself it ia hardly to be wondered at that Mr. Crone should be eintradieted by Lord Beaconefield when his lordship attempts to give hie version of the . business. As for Lord Salisbury—why, it is said, that lying has become with him one of the fine arts. If the firmnesss of the British Government had ineintained European peace, as Mr. Crone naid at Warrington it did, what in the name of fortune did Lord 8e11430111, field mean by saying, shortly after he returned from Berlin, that he had been able to prove at the Congress, "as an absolute fact," that" this horrible devastating war would never have taken place if England had spoken with the tomeneary firmness ? ' Which of these statements are the electors to accept—that told by Mr. Cross or that told by hie chief? What are the facts P After the Crimean War it was nought to aolve the much-vexed Eastern question by establishing the principle of European concert, by granting the inde- pendence and integrity of the Turkish empire, by thrusting Russia back from the Danube, and taking promises from the Turks for the good government of their Christian subject.. Turkey neglected to keep her promise, and in August, x 975, the cry of" Liberty or death" resounded throughout Herzegovina. An insurrectionary host took the field against the Turkish troops; the cry of "Liberty or death" spread to Bosnia, and it travelled to Bulgaria, where, notwith- standing the pooh-poobilig of the Premier in his " reffee-hou. babble" eprech, outrages that would sicken barbarian. were committed. War firm were lit in Servia and Monteuegro, and ell thegreat Powers of Europe, except England, felt that it was time to interfere, and, in the interests of general peace, com- pel Turkey to carry out the pronaime she had made twenty years before. In May, 1876, England rejected the Berlin memorandum, and in January, 1877. spurned the Austrian note, because Amnia, Austria, Germany, Italy, and Franreproposed that t•efficacioce to...tures" should be taken if Turkey a-eBlB not mend her ways. Those "efficacious measures" meant the occupation of the revolted provinces by Austria, and they would have prevented the war that followed. England preferred to keep things as the:, were, and the Government's refusal to join the othm powers in coercing Turkey to act justly by het Christinst subjects precipitated war. The other powers refused to move without England, and Rust. ,hBB 8885 in effect, If you won't make Turkey be. have herself we will." She tried, and the world

knows the tenth. The fact is the policy of the present Government from first to last was that of first threatening Russia, then scolding the Turks, jand, after twice boxing the compass from extre me non-iutemention to energetie interventito, adopting • policy of conditional neutrality, tempered by era- untied bluster et liteetia end injud:citms bottleshold- • Mg for the Turka. Mr. Cross would bave the roantry to believe that the action and firmness of the Govern- ! merit kept Rusaia out of Gonstauttnople. Why Buena never intended to go to Constantinople. She promised not to annex it, but said that the "march of events" might cause lier troops to go there temporarily, not permanently. It would have been madness for her to attempt to permanently occupy Constantinople, because she knew well enough that neither England, Autria, Germany, nor Frauoe would permit her to do it. Ruseia, as is well known, never went nearer to Constantinople than Sun Stefano, 33 milto away, and she only went there with her troupe from Tchataldja whew the British fleet forced ito way through the Dardanelles in epee of the proteet of the Sultan. Two year* belore that Mr. Gladstone recommended, and the Cur hiroaelf, on the 26th September, 1076, poeitively urged that the British Let should proceed to COO stantiaople, through the Dardanelles, and compel the t Tad, to free the Bulgarians. If this had been done, • tbe British Government would have averted the war, Bulgaria would have been freed without dmtroying t the Ottoman empire. Lied Beaconsfield practically If admitted it Mr. Craiii deuiee it. Which are I t we to believe? The San Stefano treaty, about • which Mr. Cross is greatly exerciaed, was never meant by Rumia to be filiat, but only • preliminary arrangement. It was limply objectionable to the j Tory English Government bemuse it freed too many of the Slavonic um.

This inconsistencses. of the Government are no more marked than by the conduct of its plenifxftentiaries at the Berlin Congress, where they initiated on all matters affecting he Eastern question being sub- mitted to discussion by and to the approval of the representativee of the various European states, whilst at the very time Lords Beaconsfield and Salisbury had a secret treaty in their pooketa for taking over Cyprus, and breaking up the independence and integrity of the Tuikiish empire, which they had sworn to maintain And what did the Congress end in, In the public ratification of a secret agreement between Lord Salisbury and Russia, in connection with whieh there was • good deal of official lying when the agreement found its way unexpectedly into the columns sf the Were newspaper—ao agreement in which, in return for the priceless privilege uf re-enslaving the Southern Bulgarian, the English Government agreed to let RtielliA have all site fired for herself, and converting that very Russo-Turkish preliminary agreement of San Stefano, that Mr. Cross found fault with, into an interrutional treaty binding on all the powers. Arid what is the Berlin Tieaty itself I' Why a treaty of partition, dividing the Ottoman Empire between Roasia, Austria, Roumania, Praia, StrVii Montenegro, and Greece, setting up an independent Bul- garia, placing Turkey under the tutelage of Europe, and creating Eastern Roumelia. And that is what Lords Bea- consfield and Salisbury Oullel maintaining the intependence and integrity of the Turkish Empire, after obtaining, under false pretences, a rots of P 4,000,000, to enable them to put on a bold front,” and alter tbey bad ignored the authority of Parliament by bringing 7,000 Sepuys from India to Malta at roost of Sltio per man. 'The result uf all is that Turkey is permanently ruined, Belg-aria divided, Russia made mistress of A.M. Miniirand the Black Sea, ard Austria started on the road to runt, which :trelebes eastward to Constantinople. Turkey has not, and perhaps never will, fulfil the conditions affecting her under the Berlin Treaty, which was declared to have secured " peace with honour." Cyprus is a nest of fevers and unprofitable. The whole policy of the Govern- Meat has been snout theatiical sensationalism. They have resorted to lying without limit, they have violated treaties, they have tampered with the Constitution, they have lieCeiVed and dsgraded Parliament, they have involved the empire in ruinous responsibilities, and they have brought about the very danger,' they have pretend.' to prevent. They have cried vehemently against Russian aggrandise- ment, whilst they have Leen bushy engaged in shifting the landinarks of their neighbours. 'Their policy Irvin first to last bas been unjust and 1111.hieVOUS, and it is for the electors now to my whether they will haves repetition of it.

div.head: COMING ELECTIONS IN LANCASHIRE AND
div.p: THE COMING ELECTIONS IN LANCASHIRE AND
CHESHIRE.

All over Lancaehire and in portions of Cheshire the battle of the electionn is being fought with perhape greater spirit tlron in any other portion. of the kingdom. Although Lord Ramsay orf • recent occasion failed to wrest Liverpool from the Teri., the splendid tight that he mule, and the com- paratively speaking /IAIIOII/ majority by which be was defeated, were indications of A great re.awakeniug of Liberal opinion through,ut the County Palatine, end every by eines the opening of the electoral cooteet, there is froth evidence forthconiing of the strength of the Liberal reaction. flo far as Liverpool is concerned, the Liberals appear to have made up their mind. for the present to he satiefied with the minority Seat, and Lord Ramsay, whose addrees appeared a day or two ago, will be without a collemme, and sure of his return. But every- where else in Lancashire, with the exception of Bury, where Mr. H. N. Philips. the Liberal 1111.1116,0 will hare a walk over," the AAAIn of the editing inernirers have been challenged, and the political excitement is increasing to a white hoof. The .2reatest interest continue, to be centred in the North- Knot of the oounty, where the leader of the Liberal party has to contend agaioet the prejudices of a powerful Tory-Orange faction. But in the North-East, ...ell ae in the other three county division. And in the boroughs, the 'electors appear to be fully alive to the importance of the crisiethey are passing thiough,and there are many indicationo that a great change is now taking place in Lancashire opinioh. We have dealt elsewhere with the Home Score- tary's speeches and candidature, but we may here observe that the oddness with which he hes been received in many places. tea warning to him that even in his native county. his popularity loon the wane. There i.e ring of hopeful confidence in the whitensen and speeches of the Liberal can- didates that contrasts curiously with a certain despondency of tone that pervades many of the utterance. of the Ministerialista. The reception that Mr. Cross experienced ! from hie constituents during the election of. 1874, contrasts ominously with that which is now accorded to him. To make matters worse, the Liberal candidates for tiouth.W. Lancashire are every- where winning troops of friends, and indeed there are no niore formidable opponents to the Tory muse to be found, than Mew.. Itathu,ne and Molyneux are proving themselves to ! be. We have reason to believe that there are no county constituencies in England whose condition at the present I moment iecausing greater consternation and alarm in the' Tory camp, than those of North-East and Soutb-Weet Len- cashire. The probabilities appear to be entirely in favour of tbe return of Lord Harlington and his popular colleague Mr. Grafton in the North-East, and of one or both of the Liberal canditLem in the South-West. The lows of his seat by the Home Secretary and the election of the Liberal leader for an important division of a couoty that for the Last dome years has been the stronghold of Toryism, would be the most damaging defeat that the Government could possibly sustain. In the South-East division Messrs. Leake and Agnew, the Liberal candidates, are making most eatiefutory progress, and it is not too much 10 000 that they are re- I ceiving an amount of support that was hardly expected even by the must sanguine amongst their supporters and agents. Mr. If ardca-tle's seat is most assure:l:y in danger, and Mr. , Algernon Egerton hes abundant reason to feel disturbed about the result. In North Lancashire the Liberals have assailed only tone of tbe seam, and the probabilitiee are that , Mr. Storey, a Liberal, will there be returned as the col- I leage of the brother of Lord Derby. In Chmhire, we can scarcely believe that Liberal prospect. are A bright for the candidates for county reprmentation ea they are in Lancashire, and yet the accounts that cont,nue to resich us are of • most favourable character. Mr. Cornwallis Went, in West Cheshire, is meeting with warm eupport, and Intro trartere whence it was hardly to be expected. The hopes of the Liberal party are rising all over the county, and so favourable has teen the reception accnrded Mr. West that it is even alleged that at the last moment Mr. Crompton is to be asked to reconsider his decision not to contest the second seat. But, be this as it may, there is at least every prospect of the return of one Liberal candidate in 1 Ibis important division. A correspondent writes :—.The Grosvenor influence will, of course, toot the Liberal ride.' The Duke of Westminster's heir has written • letter recom- . mending hie friends in that part of the county to give the' Liberal candidate or candidates all the mainlinee they One, and HA. demonstration of sympathy will, it is certain, cost the Tories a good many votes.- In Mid-Cheshire the contest will be very keen, and on account of the well-known ability with which one of the Liberal candidates has from ment time advocated the rights of the tenant farmer, it will be watched with keen interest. Mr. Bright, in his recent epetsch a Birminghat, mid that the English county members in the Home of Commons mere, in a sense, the product of the great land monopoly of this country, and the time weo near ohmn the great land monopoly would le assailed. There is no county in England to which these words apply to sell or they do to Cheshire. It is in Mid-Cheshire that Messrs. Latham and Armitage no. leading the MIMI nor Thu greet

„ , In the course of his remarks, the lecturer said they often heard the cry. "The church in in danger.” Owing t, various things, perhaps a titan was at well outside any of the churches as inside them. That famous, or rather infamous !dogma, that there was no sal floe out of the church, Bunyan dismimed in the "Pilgrim'. Progress" in • very summary manner. The pilgrim celled Faithful was , decidedly the very best of those mentioned in the book—far I better than Christian, the hero of the story. who, probably representing the Great Dreamer himself, was not drawn in Bettering terms. Faithful passed by the Palace Beautiful, mentioned in the book, and thought by the lecturer to typify a Christian Church, and did not even think it worth while to enter. The reply given by Faithful to the question why he dirt nnt enmr, was rather of a cavalier sort, being "It wan about noon, and because I had we much Are before me I passed by it." So that, probably, the best of all Bunyan's pilgrims was not a chur.ch member at all. Thus Bunyan caves well-merited rebuke to the importance of the Church, the exaltabon of which idea had been such a source of mischief. As to Christian's remark tlmt if Faithful had emend into the palace (or church) he would have seen many rarities which he would never have fora., he could only say that the observation was for more true Oran plea. inc. He (the speaker) had himself men church m which were such rarities that he wrathi never forget tl.ein ; but though he retnembered them it was with anger contempt, and sorrow. He could only express a hope that such rarities would be more rare in the future than they had hero in the past. 'The Church ought to he the abode. according to Bunyan, of Discretion. Piety, and Charby. This waste it be, for discre ion alone would he likely to he hard and rough, and to 111.1 the noftening indnence of Piety and charity, end these, in their turn, might be foolish, and do more Couto thee good, if not aided by discretion and piety. Alas there were churches in which none of these fair graces could be found, but instead of them there were envy, hatred, and all uncharitablenees. The Church might ifleet in a barn.like place, each as Burman's old chapel in Bedford was. That mattered very little, for wherever there was a congregation, though but a small one, of true-hearted, Godly people, there, in the sight of God, watt PARC, Beautiful. Ministers were often fnund to be very urgent about people joining the church, and sorne even went so far as to sty "If you 'tenor join our church, you will be Inet;" but Buoy fl showed that he was incapable of adopting such a comae Iry making Faithful pass the portal of the palace without the knowledge and consent of the porter. Mr. Brown next referred to Vanity Fair, and to the many wares sold there, amongst which was Roman ware, to which Banyan said our English nation, and some other nations, ' had taken a dislike. ' As to immorality, the alliance of England would vie with any of the large towns In dishonesty, profaneness, imptuity, and intemperance. Much solemn nonsenee was talked about the temptations of !erne towns, as though there seem no ' temptation. elsewhere. There were jost m great temptations in rural hamlets as In any town in England. He could asinire them that it was almost always in the stnall towns and wit- lager that he heard of the inost scandalous and abominable wickedness. It Rat customary to draw a distinction between the Clturch and the congregation, bet he did not think the distinction could be drawn upon either religious or moral grounds. That WWI, he had no reason to believe that the ' Church was better than the congregation, or the concerns- ' lion better than the Church, and he opoke after 30 years of observation. He must my that he shrank with extreme loathing from the sanctimoniousness which drew the line between the Church and the congregation, an marking all the converted from the unconverted—the saved from the un- saved, and times who pleased God from these who did not please Him. That line marked all theme who bad premised much to God from those who had premised Ilion nothinn, hilt as to the performance of the promise, that line told : nething—almolutely nothing. The speaker condemned the absurd erstacies in which some talked of Heaven, as if they ' had been there 25 years and knew all al.ut it. The great , matter wan not toter Heaven very clearly in the heavens, ' hut by getting nearer and nearer to it day by day ho ! patiently pursuing the path of duty which 1.1 to it. (Ap. ' plause.) Mary had seen Heaven, and described it very eloquently many had seen a great deal more than the pilgrim raw from the Delectable Mountains, and yet had never gone thither at all! The sneaker said the Pilgrim's Progress •Ite very differently constructed boo those grimly- goody. storiem, the object nf which seemed tn be to send , Christian out of the world as noon as possible. These sort ' of tales Batty contradicted St. Paul's statement that godliness had the promise of the life that now lean well as at that ' which is to c one. Mr. Brow• concluded by a beautiful reference to the Land of Beulah and the river that had no bridge.
After a frot complimentary remarks by the (7Painhap, the proceplinge were brought t*. conclusion by the singing of the Doxology.

Haaleburet. on The link between coosciousnefte and matter." Mr. T Norman ',melded, end there WAS a fair attendance. The essay wu based entirely en the aamniption of the truth of eltrtro- biology or mesmerism, although the aystetn had been atom- elated to a Large extent with trickery, the essayist contended that it was imposdble that for more the. century, hun- dreda, nay thousanda, of decent, steady-going. revectable I peoplc who at all other times behaved themselves with propriety, ehould combine to make themselves the laughing stock of their townsfolk, and do thing. that at other times they would never dream of doing unless they were actually under some alien influence. The argument yeas that if the etrong will of a MAD could subjugate the coosciousneme of his weaker fellow to any extent, the oinnipotent wilrof lion could when brought t.m bear man our conaciousneee subjugate it entirely. It was adducet by way of example that the genet of taste could be completely changed by mesmeric power, and that the other menses were affected in proportion to itA intensity that im to say, that a sufficient power of this kind, could account for all that we call material reality. The two beliefs, one or the other of which gain the assent of all ranks and eonditioos of men, were then brought under review. First, the belief that inatter was never created at all. but was eternal. Second, the belief that God made• something out of nothing It was nhown that to suppose matter was created

by an intelligent Beitig led to th• wildest absurdities. It If to the conclusion that that which was never fashioned with now or attaining the myriad mimosa of the universe, was of its own mnselesa self tbe very I,st that an Infinite at is- dim could have made it. The second belief that God mode something not of nothing, wee perfectly incredible to the human understanding. and beyond any conceivable expan- sion of mental powers. It ,on, entirely • matter of faith, and, therefore, scarcely came within the category of theory. Theo it woe shown 11,01 10 believe that matter was eimpiy the effect of the infinite will acting upon our consciousneas, in the mine sort, though infinitely greater in a degree, that a powerful human will can subjugate the senees of an inferior, invoiced neither the absurdities of believing matter tot,. eternal nor the ruioation of our niental faculties In implicit faith. It was ehown that such a belief woe literally and precisely Scriptural. And God mid, w Let there be "—nod it was on--of His own will begat, lie as, to. Plato held three Iva. ontioooual cob- to all things material. Shakeepeare drew near to it ! when he said, "We are such stuff as dreams are made of." ! one of the most powerful German minfig of the pre- : sent century, approached it when he said the only true : reality WAN spirit and Thomas Carlyle shadowed it forth o hen be mid, "How can this earth, which is dead, and a vision, resist epirits that have reality and are alive." (Laughter.) So that, attending to Mr. Gladstone, the test question was not whether the policy of the Government had been right, but whether they would turn out the Government and then de- cide what their police should be. Leach., and cheera.) Fie (Mn. Crows) contended that if the Liberate got into power Sheen would be a•I end to their unity and they would all differ horn each other. (Laughter.)
